USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Stay the course in the advanced negotiations without escalating or over-conceding. Continue pressing for a robust, verifiable enforcement mechanism and concrete Chinese purchase/IP commitments, holding our installed $250B tariff threat as leverage until Beijing delivers, while signaling readiness to roll back tariffs as the deal closes. Avoid any new escalation that could collapse a near-complete agreement and deepen the farm-sector and growth pain.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is moderate but not existential. Tariffs on ~$250B of Chinese goods remain in place and the scheduled List 3 hike to 25% has been suspended repeatedly, so the escalation freeze is holding (event timeline, 2019-02-24, 2019-03-01). Talks are advanced and favorable to the US: Mnuchin said on Apr 10 that a policing/enforcement mechanism is 'pretty much agreed' with enforcement offices on both sides, and on Apr 13 that talks are 'nearing the final round,' with China offering fentanyl bans, cloud-market access, and ~$30B/yr agricultural purchase pledges (web: Reuters 2019-04-11, NYT 2019-04-13). This is the classic leverage posture from the USA anchor near -0.5-to-0: we are extracting concessions. That keeps the threat modest. But real costs and tail risks argue against complacency: US industrial production has softened (~1.7% decline over the window) and the 10-year Treasury yield fell from ~3.08% to ~2.53%, signaling growth/rate concerns (country_health USA); the soybean sector lost ~$7.9B with ~27.5M tons unsold and record stockpiles, generating mounting farm-belt political pressure (web: Business Insider 2019-02-25, CNN 2019-03-20). An escalation to 25% on the full $200B tranche would worsen these and was flagged by Bank of America as a potential recession trigger (web: PBS 2018-07-06). The outcome is uncertain and talks could still break down, so this reads as mildly threatening (+0.2) rather than a clear opportunity. Given the deal is within reach, escalating now would be self-defeating, while full concession would forfeit hard-won leverage and enforcement — hence hold/negotiate (action 0.0).
key_factors: Escalation freeze holding; List 3 hike to 25% repeatedly suspended
Enforcement mechanism 'pretty much agreed' — talks nearing 'final round' (Mnuchin)
China concessions: fentanyl ban, cloud access, ~$30B/yr ag purchases

US IP softening and 10Y yield decline (~3.08% to ~2.53%) signal growth concerns
Tail risk: deal breakdown could re-trigger escalation toward recession risk

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue to negotiate in good faith toward a comprehensive agreement that secures the removal of US Section 301 tariffs, without new escalation. Stay at the table through the next round(s) and a likely Trump–Xi summit, holding firm on the most intrusive structural demands (forced-tech-transfer and enforcement provisions) while signaling flexibility on purchase commitments. Do not escalate now — doing so would destroy the near-term deal and the enforcement mechanism both sides have nearly agreed. Do not concede fully either, since there is no matching US offer to lift tariffs yet.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is real but not existential. US tariffs on ~$250B of Chinese imports remain in force and are a measurable drag on the export sector (Q1 exports up only 1.4%, imports down 4.8%; Feb exports plunged ~21%, CNN/March 2019), and the Huawei/Meng episode is a live firm-level irritant (2019-01-28 DOJ, extradition request). However, the trajectory is clearly de-escalatory and knowable as of 2019-04-25: the 25% List 3 hike has been postponed twice (2019-02-24, 2019-03-01), talks produced 'unprecedented' Chinese offers on tech transfer (CNBC, 2019-03-28), Mnuchin reported the enforcement mechanism 'pretty much agreed' (Reuters, 2019-04-11), and Trump said 'we'll know over the next four weeks' with a possible summit (CNBC, 2019-04-04). Macro is stabilizing — March exports rebounded +14.2%, CNY was steady ~6.72, and the IMF held China's 2019 growth at 6.3% with stimulus cushioning. This places the threat at the high-but-manageable end (+0.4), not existential. Given the talks are advanced and genuinely progressing, the correct action is to keep negotiating (action_score ≈ +0.1): escalation would be self-defeating, and full concession is premature absent a US commitment on tariff removal.
key_factors: ~$250B US Section 301 tariffs still in force, dragging exports
Trajectory de-escalatory: 25% hike postponed twice, enforcement mechanism near-agreed
Truce holding; Trump-Xi summit in prospect (end-April timeline)
Huawei/Meng firm-level targeting an ongoing irritant
Structural demands (IP, forced tech transfer) touch CCP industrial policy, hard to concede fully
Macro stabilizing: March exports +14.2%, CNY ~6.72, IMF holds China at 6.3%
China has already made unprecedented concessions (tech transfer, farm purchases, fentanyl ban)
